slots.X: A hypothetical M₂O₃ oxide of mass 4.08 g is quantitatively converted to dry NaMO₂ (6.56 g), with no impurity or loss. Infer M atomic mass, then calculate the volume of 0.80 mol/L HCl needed for 2.04 g of the same oxide. Explain why the isolated formula cannot automatically be used as aqueous speciation.
slots.Y: An inverse mass balance can identify an oxide when a defined anhydrous product is isolated quantitatively. For ideal M₂O₃ → 2NaMO₂, the two products contain the original two M atoms and add a net 62 g per mole of oxide (2Na + O). A sample of 3.00 g giving 4.86 g product therefore represents 0.030 mol oxide, with molar mass 100 g/mol and M atomic mass 26. This is a hypothetical element mass, not a claim about a real oxide. In acid, one formula unit consumes 6 H⁺; 0.030 mol oxide consumes 0.180 mol H⁺. In aqueous base the actual species can be hydroxo complexes; the anhydrous formula applies only to the isolated product under the model. Check masses, charge and isolation assumptions separately.
slots.Z: Mass gain 2.48 g = 62 g/mol × oxide amount, so .040 mol. Oxide molar mass 102, M=27. A 2.04 g portion is .020 mol, consumes .120 mol H⁺; volume .120/.80=.150 L. In strong aqueous base hydroxo species may exist; dry NaMO₂ is an isolated-product assumption. Atom and charge ledger: M₂O₃+6H⁺→2M³⁺+3H₂O.
slots.W: Infer oxide amount from independent mass gain before using acid equivalents; distinguish phase-specific species.
